isaiah-53-rabbinic-messianic-reading.d: Isaiah 53 describes a man called God's servant. He is hated and rejected. He is wounded and killed. He is buried with the rich. Then he sees light and is satisfied. Christians have pointed to this chapter for two thousand years.

Most Jewish people today read the servant as the nation of Israel, not one man. Israel suffered at the hands of the nations. So the chapter is about a people, not a person. It is a serious reading and it deserves a real answer.

isaiah-53-rabbinic-messianic-reading.t: The part most Christians don't know
isaiah-53-rabbinic-messianic-reading.d: That reading became standard fairly late. Older Jewish sources read the chapter as being about the Messiah. The Targum is the ancient Aramaic version read aloud in synagogues. It opens the passage this way: "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper." The Talmud and several medieval rabbis go the same direction.
Very. This is graded conceded because the evidence comes from Jewish sources, not Christian ones. Nobody has to trust our reading. They can look it up in their own tradition.

It changes the whole shape of the conversation. You are not telling a Jewish person what their book means. You are asking about something inside their own tradition. That is a completely different kind of talk.
"Did you know the Targum on this chapter calls the servant the Messiah? I'd love to read it with you."

isaiah-53-servant-distinct-from-israel.d: If the servant in Isaiah 53 is the nation of Israel, the Christian reading falls apart. So the whole thing turns on one question. Does the chapter treat the servant as the nation, or as someone separate from it?

First, verse 8 says the servant was struck "for the transgression of my people." That is hard if the servant is that people. A group cannot be punished for the sins of itself. Second, verse 9 says he had done no violence and told no lies. The prophets never say that about Israel. They say the opposite, constantly.

isaiah-53-servant-distinct-from-israel.t: Being fair to the other side
isaiah-53-servant-distinct-from-israel.d: Isaiah does call Israel God's servant elsewhere, in chapters 41, 44 and 49. That is true and worth saying out loud. So the word "servant" alone settles nothing. The argument has to come from chapter 53 itself.
Strong. Counter-missionary writers usually shift to the other chapters instead of answering verse 8 directly. Ask about verse 8 and wait.
This is the hinge of the most-discussed chapter in the whole conversation. Get it right and everything downstream is steadier.
"Read me verse 8. Who is the servant being struck for?"

sukkah-52a-two-messiahs.d: The Hebrew Bible seems to describe the coming one twice, in ways that do not fit. One picture is a king from David's line who wins and rules in peace. The other is a servant who is hated, pierced and killed. Both are there. They look impossible to combine.

This is not a Christian observation. The Talmud faces the same problem and solves it with two Messiahs. Messiah son of Joseph suffers and is killed. Messiah son of David reigns. That solution exists because the problem is genuinely in the text.

The Christian claim is smaller than it sounds. Not two figures, but one figure, twice. He came the first time as the servant. He comes again as the king. Every part of the rabbinic solution is kept. Only the arithmetic changes.
Very. This is graded conceded because the two-portrait problem is admitted inside Judaism itself, in one of its own central texts.
It moves the argument off "your book says" and onto a shared puzzle. You are both looking at the same difficulty. You just count differently.
"How do you read Sukkah 52a? Why is one person twice harder than two people once?"

daniel-9-cut-off-before-destruction.d: Almost any prophecy can be placed somewhere in history if you try hard enough. That is why arguing about them rarely settles anything. Daniel 9 is different. It has an order of events with an end point.
An anointed one is cut off. Only after that do the people of a coming ruler destroy the city and the sanctuary. The sanctuary is the Second Temple in Jerusalem. Rome destroyed it in AD 70.

The arithmetic of the seventy weeks is genuinely argued about. There are several ways to count them and no agreement. Do not pretend otherwise. But the order of events does not depend on the arithmetic. The anointed one comes first. The Temple falls second. The Temple is gone.
Contested, and we say so. The sequence is strong. The date maths is not settled. Lead with the sequence and concede the maths.
It is the one prophecy on this page with a deadline that has already passed. That makes it checkable in a way the others are not.
"Daniel says an anointed one is cut off before the sanctuary is destroyed. The Temple fell in AD 70. Who was that?"

micah-5-2-bethlehem.d: Micah wrote in the 700s BC. He says a ruler over Israel will come out of Bethlehem. He calls the town small, which it was. Then he adds that this ruler's "goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting."
The verse claims a specific birthplace. It also claims an origin that comes before the birth. The first part is simple. The second part is where the argument is.

Counter-missionary writers focus on the second half. They argue the Hebrew means ancient lineage — a family line going back a long way — not existence from eternity. That is a fair question about the words, and the Hebrew genuinely can carry that sense.
Contested. The birthplace part is solid. The "from everlasting" part is a real translation debate, and a Christian who pretends it isn't will lose credibility fast.
Used carefully it adds weight. Used as a knockout blow it invites a correction you cannot answer.
"How do you read the second half of Micah 5:2? I've heard it taken two ways."

zechariah-12-10-pierced.d: Zechariah describes a day when God pours out grace on Jerusalem. Then comes the strange part. "They shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him." The sentence shifts from "me" to "him" partway through.

zechariah-12-10-pierced.t: It is odd before anyone argues
zechariah-12-10-pierced.d: That shift is in the Hebrew itself. It is not a Christian translation trick. Jewish commentators have wrestled with it for centuries, because God is speaking and yet the mourning is for someone else.

The strongest thing here is not Christian commentary. It is Jewish commentary. The Talmud connects this mourning to a slain Messiah — Messiah son of Joseph. Again, that reading comes from inside the tradition.
Graded conceded. You can make this argument entirely from Jewish sources, which is the only kind of argument that travels here.
A pierced figure who is mourned, in a Jewish prophet, read by Jewish sages as a Messiah who dies. That is a lot to explain away.
"Why does this verse switch from 'me' to 'him'? And what did the sages make of it?"

psalm-22-pierced-hands-feet.d: Psalm 22 opens with the words Jesus quoted from the cross. It describes a man surrounded by enemies. His bones are out of joint. People stare at him. They divide his clothing by casting lots. It was written centuries before crucifixion was used in Judea.

Verse 16 is the argument. The standard Hebrew text reads something like "like a lion, my hands and my feet." The ancient Greek translation reads "they pierced my hands and my feet." One Hebrew letter separates the two readings, and they are easy to confuse by eye.

A fragment found at Nahal Hever, near the Dead Sea, supports the piercing reading. It is roughly a thousand years older than the standard Hebrew text we normally use. That matters, but it is one fragment, and honest scholars still disagree.
Contested, and this is a case where saying so is the whole point. A Christian who claims verse 16 obviously says "pierced" will be corrected, and will deserve it.
The rest of the psalm needs no textual argument at all. The staring, the mocking, the divided clothing and the casting of lots are not disputed by anyone.
"Set verse 16 aside — it's a real textual question. Read me the rest of the psalm."

genesis-49-10-shiloh.d: Jacob is dying. He blesses his twelve sons one by one. To Judah he says the sceptre will not depart from him "until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be."

genesis-49-10-shiloh.t: Nobody is sure what Shiloh means
genesis-49-10-shiloh.d: That is worth admitting up front. It is one of the genuinely obscure words in the Hebrew Bible. Proposed meanings include "the one to whom it belongs," a place name, and a title. Ancient Jewish translations read it as a name for the Messiah.

The verse ties Judah's governing authority to a deadline. So the question becomes historical rather than linguistic. When did Judah's ruling power actually end? That is something you can look up together.
Contested. The messianic reading is ancient and Jewish, which is a point in its favour. The obscure word and the disputed history keep it from being settled.
It is one of the oldest passages read as messianic by Jews themselves, long before there was any argument with Christians about it.
"The Targum reads Shiloh as the Messiah. What do you make of that?"

isaiah-7-14-almah.d: "A virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." You have heard it read every December. It is also the weakest of the famous Christian proof-texts, and this page says so plainly.

The Hebrew word is almah. It means a young woman of marrying age. The specific Hebrew word for virgin is betulah, and Isaiah did not use it. So the translation "virgin" is doing more work than the Hebrew requires.

Read the whole chapter. Isaiah is giving a sign to King Ahaz about a war that was about to end. The child is a sign within that crisis. A prophecy about someone born seven centuries later would not have helped Ahaz at all.

Jewish translators rendered almah as parthenos — the Greek word for virgin — in the Septuagint, around 250 BC. No Christian influenced that. And Matthew is reading the verse as a pattern being filled out, not as a prediction with one meaning.
Contested, and handle it as typology or leave it alone. Conceding this one is what earns you a hearing on Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9, which actually hold.
"I'll be honest — I don't think this verse works the way it's usually preached."

second-temple-messianic-expectation.d: A common claim is that Christians invented the Messiah they wanted, then read him backwards into the Hebrew Bible. It sounds reasonable. It is also checkable, because we have Jewish writings from before Jesus was born.

second-temple-messianic-expectation.t: What the Dead Sea Scrolls show
second-temple-messianic-expectation.d: A fragment known as 4Q521 describes a Messiah under whom the blind see and the dead are raised. It is Jewish. It is pre-Christian. And it is almost word for word the answer Jesus later sends back to John the Baptist in Matthew 11.

The Psalms of Solomon, written about a century before Jesus, describe a Davidic king who will cleanse Jerusalem and gather the tribes. The expectation was alive, specific, and datable. It was not invented after the fact.
Graded conceded. These are Jewish documents, dated by scholars with no stake in the Christian conclusion.
It removes the "you made it up afterwards" objection before it can be raised, using evidence that came out of the ground in 1947.
"Have you read 4Q521? It sounds a lot like Matthew 11, and it's older."

jeremiah-31-new-covenant.d: One of the most common things you will hear is simple. Christianity invented a "new covenant" to replace the one God made with Israel. It gets said as if it were obviously a Christian idea.

The phrase is not Christian. It is Jeremiah's. He is a Hebrew prophet writing to Jewish people. And he says God will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. He names them both.
A law written on the heart rather than on stone. Everyone knowing God directly, from the least to the greatest. And sins forgiven and remembered no more. None of that is imported from outside.
Strong. There is no good reply to this one. The text sits in the Tanakh and it names its own parties.
It dissolves the "you invented a different religion" frame before it can form. You are pointing at a Jewish promise, not a Christian claim.
"Who is Jeremiah's new covenant made with? Read me verse 31."

yoma-39b-forty-years.t: How the Day of Atonement worked
yoma-39b-forty-years.d: Once a year the high priest drew lots between two goats. A crimson thread was said to turn white when the sacrifice was accepted. And a lamp in the Temple burned as a sign that God was present. These were the signs everyone watched for.

The Talmud says that for the forty years before the Temple was destroyed, the signs stopped working. The lot no longer came up in the right hand. The thread stopped turning white. The westernmost lamp went out.
The Temple was destroyed in AD 70. Forty years before that is AD 30. That is the traditional date of the crucifixion.
Graded conceded, because this is not a Christian source. It is one of Judaism's own central texts, describing its own Temple, and nobody disputes that the passage says what it says.
It is the single most striking thing on this page, and you never have to argue for it. You only have to ask someone to read it.
"Would you look up Yoma 39b with me? I'd like to know how you read it."

atonement-after-the-temple.d: Leviticus 17:11 is direct. "It is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul." Atonement happens through blood placed on an altar. That altar stood in the Temple in Jerusalem.
Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70. The altar has been gone for nineteen centuries. Whatever else changed that year, the thing Leviticus names as the means of atonement stopped existing.

With prayer, repentance and acts of kindness. This is a serious, ancient and deeply thought-through answer, developed by people facing a catastrophe. Treat it with respect. Rabbinic Judaism has carried it for a very long time.
It is still worth asking once, gently. The Torah names blood on an altar. The rabbinic answer names something else. Where does the Torah authorise the replacement? Ask it, then stop talking.
Contested. The question is real and hard. The Jewish answer is not stupid, and treating it as stupid will end the conversation.
"Leviticus grounds atonement in blood on an altar. What grounds it now?"

hosea-blindness-restoration-romans-11.d: A Christian has to deal with what Christians have done. The Crusades. The blood libel. The expulsions from England and Spain. Forced disputations. Luther. Then Christian Europe between 1941 and 1945.

Romans 11 is where. Paul asks whether God has cast away his people and answers "God forbid." He describes a blindness that is partial and temporary. He says the calling of Israel cannot be revoked. He promises a certain restoration.

Paul tells Gentile believers they are a branch grafted into someone else's tree. Then he warns them, directly, not to boast against the root. The arrogance that produced a thousand years of violence is condemned in the New Testament itself.
Strong. There is no serious reading of Romans 11 that supports contempt, and Christians who held one were reading against their own book.
Say this unprompted, before you open any other text. Your friend has spent their life waiting for a Christian who says it without being pushed.
"I know what the word Christian has meant to Jewish families. I'm not going to pretend otherwise."

nt-jewish-library.d: Many Jewish people meet the New Testament one way. It is the book of the religion that hurt their families. That makes it very hard to read as anything else. The reaction is earned.

Set the history aside for a moment and look at the books. They were written almost entirely by Jews. They argue from the Hebrew Scriptures. They are about a Jewish teacher. They were written within a few decades of the events, largely for Jewish audiences.

This is not a Christian talking point. A great deal of modern Jewish scholarship says the same thing. Amy-Jill Levine helped edit the Jewish Annotated New Testament. Daniel Boyarin argues that a divine, suffering Messiah was already a Jewish idea.
Graded conceded. Jewish scholars say it, and they have no stake in the Christian conclusion.
You are not asking anyone to stop being Jewish. The first followers of Jesus kept the feasts. They argued from the Tanakh in synagogues.
"Have you read Levine's Jewish Annotated New Testament? I'd be interested what you think."

avoid-talmud-quote-mining.d: Lists of shocking quotations attributed to the Talmud circulate widely. They are easy to find and they look damning. Do not use them.
Most are made up, mistranslated, or cut off from the words around them. The Talmud is a huge record of debate. It keeps the losing side of an argument on the page, right next to the winning side.
Most of these lists go back to the Middle Ages. They were written for forced public debates, to justify what came next. That is the company you keep when you repeat them.
If you cannot read the passage in context on Sefaria, do not use it. That is a thirty-second check, and your friend can do it faster than you can.
If you have used one: "I repeated something about the Talmud once that turned out to be fake. I stopped."

avoid-jews-killed-jesus.d: Most entries on this list are about losing an argument. This one is about something worse. The deicide charge is the specific theological claim behind a thousand years of massacre.
The Rhineland killings in 1096. The blood libel born at Norwich in 1144. Easter pogroms. Expulsions. And a vocabulary that was still being used in the twentieth century.

A Roman prefect ordered the execution, and Rome carried it out. The New Testament's own account spreads the responsibility very differently — and Jesus says plainly that no one takes his life from him.
If any version of this phrase is in your vocabulary, take it out permanently. Not softened. Out.
Nothing. This is one to never say, not one to say better.

avoid-legalism-caricature.d: Somewhere along the way you probably heard that Judaism is about earning God's favour by rule-keeping, and that Jesus and Paul replaced it with grace. It is a tidy story. It is also wrong.

E. P. Sanders took this caricature apart in 1977, and the field moved. Second-Temple Judaism was a religion of covenant grace with obligations attached — you are in by God's choice, and you live accordingly.
Repeating it tells your Jewish friend that you have never actually asked them what they believe. You are arguing with a cartoon, and they can tell.
Ask. "How would you describe the relationship between grace and obedience?" You will learn something, and you will be trusted with the answer.
"What do you actually believe about how a person stands right with God?"

avoid-gematria-bible-codes.d: Gematria assigns numbers to Hebrew letters and adds them up. Bible codes claim that skipping letters at fixed intervals reveals hidden messages. Both get used in Christian outreach as if they were evidence.

The same techniques were run on Moby-Dick and War and Peace. They produced equally striking "predictions," including assassinations. Any long text will do this, because the method finds patterns rather than testing them.
Using them tells a thoughtful person that you cannot tell a pattern from a proof. Every real argument you make afterwards gets discounted.
Drop them entirely. The case from Isaiah 53, Daniel 9 and Yoma 39b does not need help from numerology, and is weakened by the association.
"I don't use the codes stuff. I don't think it holds up, and it isn't needed."
